claims.text: Chemical dealloying can produce high-entropy-alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Chemical dealloying selectively dissolves less noble components from noble-metal-based HEA precursors.
Selective dissolution generates a porous, interconnected structure.
The resulting porous structure provides enhanced catalytic surfaces.
The proposed precursor is a homogeneous noble-metal-based HEA containing both noble and less noble metals.
A suitable chemical etchant can selectively remove the less noble elements.
Controlling etching temperature, etchant concentration, and duration can enable selective dissolution without compromising framework integrity.
Removal of less noble atoms mediates the formation of nanoscale pores.
Removal of less noble atoms mediates the formation of a three-dimensional interconnected architecture.
During dealloying, less noble metals are corroded and leached from the precursor.
Leaching of less noble metals leaves a network of more noble metal atoms.
Dealloying increases surface area and exposes additional catalytically active sites.
The dealloyed material will form a porous three-dimensional nanoframework with high surface area.
The dealloyed nanoframework will exhibit enhanced catalytic activity relative to non-dealloyed structures.
Traditional NM-HEA synthesis methods without selective dealloying typically produce denser, less porous structures with lower accessible surface areas.
Dealloying efficiency and nanoframework uniformity depend on the initial alloy composition and dealloying parameters.
Extreme dealloying conditions may cause incomplete framework formation or structural collapse.
